headline: Reggie Watts Dropped From Festivals and Podcast After Rolling Stone Investigation Into Girlfriend's Death
deck: The musician and comedian faces professional fallout following claims about his late girlfriend's death and his public advocacy for ketamine.
body: Reggie Watts has been removed from multiple festivals and his theme song was scrubbed from the 'Comedy Bang! Bang!' podcast after Rolling Stone published an investigation into allegations surrounding his late girlfriend’s death and drug use. The investigation, which examines Watts’ relationship with his former partner and his public advocacy of ketamine, has triggered immediate professional consequences. Multiple outlets, including Consequence of Sound and Variety, have confirmed his removal from upcoming appearances and the discontinuation of his podcast theme. Watts, known for his absurdist humor and musical performances, now faces a reputational crisis that has upended his public career.

The Rolling Stone report, titled 'Reggie Watts Is a Prominent Ketamine Advocate. Was It His Ex’s ‘Undoing’?', centers on the 2017 death of his girlfriend, artist and designer Aurora Booth, whose body was found in a Los Angeles apartment. While the official cause of death was ruled an accident involving multiple drugs, including heroin and fentanyl, the investigation revisits the circumstances and implicates Watts’ influence and public promotion of ketamine, a dissociative anesthetic with growing off-label use in wellness and psychedelic therapy circles. Booth’s family has not publicly commented on the renewed scrutiny, but the timing of the investigation—nearly seven years after her death—has sparked renewed public interest in the case.

Watts, who rose to prominence as a musical guest on The Late Late Show with Craig Ferguson and as a recurring cast member on Comedy Bang! Bang!, has publicly denied any wrongdoing. In a statement to PennLive.com, he called the allegations 'dangerously false' and said they misrepresented both his relationship with Booth and his personal stance on drug use. 'I loved Aurora deeply, and her loss remains a profound tragedy for me and everyone who knew her,' Watts said. 'These claims are not only false—they are an attack on her memory and on the truth.' The statement reflects a rare moment of personal gravity in Watts’ typically playful public persona.

The professional fallout has been swift and severe. Consequence of Sound reported that Watts was dropped from at least two major festival lineups without public explanation, though sources cited the Rolling Stone investigation as the decisive factor. Meanwhile, Variety confirmed that the theme song composed and performed by Watts for Comedy Bang! Bang!, a long-running comedy podcast, has been removed from all episodes and promotional materials. The move signals a deliberate distancing by the show’s producers and platform, which has not issued an official statement but appears to be severing ties in response to the ongoing scrutiny.

The investigation also highlights Watts’ public advocacy for ketamine, which he has discussed in interviews and social media as a tool for creativity and personal insight. While ketamine has shown therapeutic promise in clinical settings for depression and PTSD, its unregulated use has raised concerns among medical professionals and addiction specialists. Watts’ promotion of the drug, particularly in the context of Booth’s death, has drawn scrutiny from those who argue that public figures must exercise greater caution when discussing substances linked to overdose risks.

This is not the first time a public figure has faced professional consequences tied to a partner’s death. In recent years, several artists and influencers have been dropped from projects or canceled following investigations into personal misconduct or substance use. The difference here is the intersection of advocacy and tragedy—Watts’ public persona as a ketamine advocate has become entangled with the circumstances of Booth’s death, creating a feedback loop of scrutiny that has accelerated the fallout.

For Watts, a performer whose career thrived on surreal detachment and absurdist detachment, the investigation represents a collision between his public brand and private life. His signature style—meandering musical improvisations, deadpan delivery, and futuristic persona—has always relied on ambiguity and irony. Now, those same qualities are being tested in a court of public opinion that demands clarity, accountability, and moral consistency.

The story is far from resolved. Watts has not been charged with any crime, and the Los Angeles County Coroner’s report from 2017 remains unchanged. But the renewed attention, fueled by Rolling Stone’s investigation, has already reshaped his professional landscape. Festivals are reconsidering bookings. Podcasts are editing archives. And a community that once embraced his eccentricity is now asking whether the cost of his art was someone else’s life.
